variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Docker is a platform for building, distributing, and running applications as containers. An image is an immutable package of application files, dependencies, and runtime metadata. A container is a runnable instance of that image plus process, network, storage, resource, and security configuration.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Core invariant”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Describe the build
pairs.detail: Order instructions so stable inputs can stay cached, and use stages to keep build-only tools out of the runtime artifact.
pairs.explanation: Order instructions so stable inputs can stay cached, and use stages to keep build-only tools out of the runtime artifact.

pairs.label: Package immutable files
pairs.detail: An image is content-addressed, read-only, and composed of filesystem layers plus configuration such as its default command and user.
pairs.explanation: An image is content-addressed, read-only, and composed of filesystem layers plus configuration such as its default command and user.

pairs.label: Run one isolated process
pairs.detail: Docker creates a writable layer and configures namespaces, control groups, mounts, and networking around the image's process.
pairs.explanation: Docker creates a writable layer and configures namespaces, control groups, mounts, and networking around the image's process.

pairs.label: Store and distribute
pairs.detail: A registry stores image manifests and layers.
pairs.explanation: A registry stores image manifests and layers. Deploy by immutable digest when the exact artifact matters; a mutable tag is only a reference.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Treat the image as a versioned delivery artifact and the container as a replaceable process.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Docker is a platform for building, distributing, and running applications as containers. An image is an immutable package of application files, dependencies, and runtime metadata. A container is a runnable instance of that image plus process, network, storage, resource, and security configuration.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Containers are not small virtual machines”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Container boundary
pairs.detail: Containers isolate processes and selected kernel resources.
pairs.explanation: Containers isolate processes and selected kernel resources. Multiple Linux containers on one host use that host's Linux kernel, so kernel compatibility and host hardening remain part of the security model.

pairs.label: Virtual-machine boundary
pairs.detail: A virtual machine presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system with its own kernel.
pairs.explanation: A virtual machine presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system with its own kernel. Teams commonly run containers inside VMs to combine deployment density with a stronger infrastructure boundary.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Treat the image as a versioned delivery artifact and the container as a replaceable process.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Container boundary: Containers isolate processes and selected kernel resources. Virtual-machine boundary: A virtual machine presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system with its own kernel.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Docker is a platform for building, distributing, and running applications as containers. An image is an immutable package of application files, dependencies, and runtime metadata. A container is a runnable instance of that image plus process, network, storage, resource, and security configuration.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Operate the process as disposable, not invisible”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Build and prove
pairs.detail: Create the image from reviewed inputs.
pairs.explanation: Create the image from reviewed inputs. Run tests, inspect dependencies, scan the final artifact, and retain provenance for the immutable digest.

pairs.label: Configure and start
pairs.detail: Inject environment-specific configuration and secrets at runtime.
pairs.explanation: Inject environment-specific configuration and secrets at runtime. Declare user, mounts, network, limits, health behavior, and restart policy before the process starts.

pairs.label: Observe and drain
pairs.detail: Collect standard output and error, application metrics, container resource signals, and events.
pairs.explanation: Collect standard output and error, application metrics, container resource signals, and events. On shutdown, stop admission, finish bounded work, and exit before the grace period expires.

pairs.label: Replace and recover
pairs.detail: Recreate from the same image and policy, attach declared persistent state, and verify service plus data recovery.
pairs.explanation: Recreate from the same image and policy, attach declared persistent state, and verify service plus data recovery. Roll back by digest when the artifact is the fault.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Treat the image as a versioned delivery artifact and the container as a replaceable process.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Build and prove: Create the image from reviewed inputs. Configure and start: Inject environment-specific configuration and secrets at runtime. Observe and drain: Collect standard output and error, application metrics, container resource signals, and events. Replace and recover: Recreate from the same image and policy, attach declared persistent state, and verify service plus data recovery.

variants.prompt: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is an immutable package; a container is a runnable instance with runtime configuration and a writable layer
An image is a running process and a container is its source repository
They are two names for the same mutable filesystem
A container always contains a complete guest operating-system kernel
variants.explanation: The image supplies read-only filesystem layers and metadata. Docker creates a container from that image plus runtime settings, isolation, and a container-specific writable layer.
optionFeedback: The image supplies read-only filesystem layers and metadata. Docker creates a container from that image plus runtime settings, isolation, and a container-specific writable layer.

variants.hint: Think about the key idea first: Docker matters because one identified image can move through development, CI, and production without rebuilding the application differently in each environment.

variants.prompt: A database writes only to its container writable layer. What happens when that container is removed and replaced?
options: Docker attaches the old writable layer automatically
The data is copied into the image registry
The old writable layer is removed and the replacement starts without that data
The data becomes a named volume
variants.explanation: The writable layer belongs to one container. Durable database files need storage whose lifecycle is independent, such as a managed volume with an explicit backup plan.

variants.prompt: Why use a BuildKit secret mount instead of ARG or ENV for a build credential?
options: Secret mounts make the credential temporarily available to one build instruction without persisting it in the final image
ARG values are always encrypted in image history
ENV values disappear before the next layer
Secret mounts publish the credential to the registry
variants.explanation: Docker documents build arguments and environment variables as inappropriate for secrets because they can persist. A secret mount exposes the value only for the consuming instruction.

variants.prompt: Why copy dependency manifests before application source in a Dockerfile?
options: It encrypts the source tree
A source-only edit can preserve the cached dependency-install layer
It makes every build ignore the lockfile
It puts development dependencies outside every image automatically
variants.explanation: Docker invalidates a changed layer and dependent layers after it. Isolating stable dependency inputs lets frequent source changes begin invalidation later.

variants.prompt: When is a bind mount a better semantic fit than a named volume?
options: When a host tool and the container must both edit a specific host path
When the workload must avoid host-path coupling
When data must disappear on stop
Whenever an image should contain a secret
variants.explanation: A bind mount deliberately exposes a daemon-host path. That is useful for source editing, but it couples the container to host layout and permissions.

options: The container is automatically limited to 512 MB
The container can use memory allowed by the host kernel and may contribute to host OOM pressure

The image size becomes the memory limit
